meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker. First documented in 1965 as a motto embroidered on a pillow in Alice Roosevelt Longworth's Washington sitting room.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If You Can't Say Something Good About Someone, Sit Right Here by Me'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dorothy Parker. A reporter recorded it in 1965 on a pillow in Alice Roosevelt Longworth's sitting room. She popularised it; the author is unknown.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1884–1980 · Theodore Roosevelt’s eldest daughter and Washington political hostess
answer.sourceLine: The pillow is genuinely hers, and the wording is documented in her own house in this exact form. The earliest known record is a Saturday Evening Post profile of Longworth, 4 December 1965, transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, in which the reporter describes a pillow on a chair in her sitting room embroidered with the words. What no source establishes is authorship — no source records her composing the line, and Quote Investigator concludes only that she “definitely popularized the expression, and she may have crafted it.” It is not Dorothy Parker’s.

source.heading: The 1965 sighting

Embroidered on a pillow in Longworth’s upstairs sitting room. Not a recorded spoken remark: a November 1966 New York Times item says she sewed the motto onto the pillow, but no source records her composing the line.
Undetermined. Quote Investigator finds she “definitely popularized the expression, and she may have crafted it.”

source.excerpt: … on one of the chairs was a pillow with the words, IF YOU CAN’T SAY SOMETHING GOOD ABOUT SOMEONE, SIT RIGHT HERE BY ME.
trail: 4 December 1965 — the first record. A Saturday Evening Post profile describes the embroidered pillow in Longworth’s sitting room, in this exact wording. Wikipedia’s “Wit” section ↗ carries the pillow line and cites Quote Investigator for the same Post page (238:24, p. 32) — the same source seen twice, not a second attestation.

1966 — it escapes the house. Quote Investigator documents a July 1966 Earl Wilson column with a “nice” variant credited to an unnamed hostess, then two November 1966 reports — in a Syracuse newspaper and The New York Times — of a Washington party guide reprinting the pillow’s words, each dated and cited ↗.

The pillow is independently attested. The Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ states that “at her tea table she kept a pillow which read, ‘If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.’”
1988 onward — the credit slips. A version reached the stage in Steel Magnolias, and by the 1990s the joke was being handed to Dorothy Parker; a historian’s fact-check rejects that credit ↗.
source.excerptNote: The reporter’s description of Longworth’s sitting room, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. Two details are worth keeping: the pillow rendered the line in capitals, and it used good — the near-universal nice is a later drift.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full dated citation trail

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for this line with confidence. Its own authorship is undetermined — Quote Investigator finds the originator’s identity not certain ↗ — so there is no identifiable author or first publication to date it from. Separately, the article in which it was first recorded appeared in The Saturday Evening Post of 4 December 1965, so its copyright renewed automatically and it remains protected; we quote only the short evidentiary sentence from it. Nothing here supports treating the line as public domain.

author.name: Alice Roosevelt Longworth
author.heading: Who was Alice Roosevelt Longworth?
author.metaLine: 1884–1980 · Washington hostess, political operator and celebrated wit
author.bio: The eldest child of Theodore Roosevelt, born in 1884 and orphaned of her mother two days later, Alice was a celebrity First Daughter who smoked on the White House roof and married Representative Nicholas Longworth of Ohio — later Speaker of the House — in a White House wedding in 1906. She outlived the marriage, her father’s party and most of her targets, running a Dupont Circle salon for six decades where, as the Theodore Roosevelt Center puts it, “views were exchanged and deals struck.” Her reputation rested on the short, lethal line — after a double mastectomy she called herself “Washington’s only topless octogenarian.” She died in 1980 at ninety-six, by then nicknamed the other Washington monument.

cite.sourceCitation: Jean vanden Heuvel, “The Sharpest Wit in Washington,” The Saturday Evening Post 238, no. 24 (December 4, 1965), start p. 30, quote p. 32 — the earliest documented appearance, describing the line as embroidered on a pillow in Alice Roosevelt Longworth’s sitting room. Citation details as given in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: If You Can’t Say Something Good About Someone, Sit Right Here by Me” (August 9, 2014).

copyAttribution: If you can't say something good about someone, sit right here by me. — attributed to Alice Roosevelt Longworth (1884–1980). Earliest documented as a motto embroidered on a pillow in her Washington sitting room, reported in The Saturday Evening Post, 4 December 1965; the originator is not certain. Commonly misattributed to Dorothy Parker, for which there is no substantive evidence. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably mis-credited jokes in American English. The confusion is understandable — it sounds like a line from the Algonquin Round Table — but the paper trail runs through a Washington drawing room, not a New York hotel.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states flatly that there is “no substantive evidence that Dorothy Parker employed the saying though it has been attributed to her in recent decades,” and dates the drift to the 1990s: a 1998 letter to the San Francisco Chronicle credited Parker and drew an editor’s correction. The historian behind Professor Buzzkill ↗ agrees: “isn’t one of hers.” Parker’s own Wikiquote page ↗, which carries a substantial Misattributed section, does not list the line at all.

Months after the pillow was first described in print, the syndicated columnist Earl Wilson ran a “sit next to me” version and credited it not to Longworth but to the unnamed hostess of a society dinner — the first sign of the line detaching from its owner, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

Robert Harling put a version of the quip in a character’s mouth, and a 1988 review of the New York production quoted her drawling it. The shortest wording is in wide circulation after this point, though no source traces the two — note that AZQuotes still files the Steel Magnolias phrasing under Dorothy Parker ↗, tagged “Magnolias.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented instance of this line is a pillow in Alice Roosevelt Longworth’s sitting room, described in The Saturday Evening Post of 4 December 1965 — and the pillow said good, not nice. She popularised it; who first composed it is not certain ↗.

context.heading: Why a pillow is better evidence than most quotes get
lead: Alice Roosevelt Longworth spent six decades as the most quotable private citizen in Washington. The Theodore Roosevelt Center ↗ records that she hosted a salon at her Dupont Circle home “where views were exchanged and deals struck,” drawing scientists, authors, diplomats and politicians of all persuasions — and that “at her tea table she kept a pillow which read, ‘If you can’t say something good about someone, sit right here by me.’”

That is a sturdier paper trail than most famous quips ever get: not a remembered remark passed down third-hand, but a physical object in a documented room, described in print by a named journalist in a datable magazine. What it cannot settle is who composed the sentence in the first place. A reporter recorded the pillow, and a November 1966 New York Times item says Longworth sewed the motto onto it; nobody recorded her composing the words. Quote Investigator ↗ stops precisely there — she “may have crafted it” — and so do we.
context.detailsSummary: How the line escaped her sitting room
detailsBody: Once a journalist printed it, the motto travelled fast. Quote Investigator documents a July 1966 Earl Wilson column carrying a “sit next to me” version credited to an unnamed party hostess, and two separate November 1966 write-ups — in a Syracuse newspaper and in The New York Times — of a Women’s National Democratic Club party guide that reprinted the pillow’s wording. Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among her quotes citing Time of 9 December 1966, the same season.

The wording loosened as it spread. The pillow said good; the newspaper versions said nice; the theatre version dropped “about someone” altogether. By the time it was a household joke, most people were quoting a paraphrase of a paraphrase — and crediting the wrong woman.
context.pull: The earliest record is not something she said. It is something a reporter saw sitting on a chair.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest evidence is a Saturday Evening Post profile of 4 December 1965 (vol. 238, no. 24, start p. 30, quote p. 32) by Jean vanden Heuvel describing a pillow reading 'IF YOU CAN'T SAY SOMETHING GOOD ABOUT SOMEONE, SIT RIGHT HERE BY ME'; Longworth 'definitely popularized the expression, and she may have crafted it'; the originator's identity is not certain; there is 'no substantive evidence that Dorothy Parker employed the saying'; July 1966 Earl Wilson column credited an unnamed hostess; November 1966 Syracuse Herald-American and New York Times reprints; 1988 Steel Magnolias review; 1998 San Francisco Chronicle letter crediting Parker drew an editor's correction.

Wikipedia's 'Wit' section states the comment 'was embroidered on a throw pillow in her Washington home: "If you can't say something good about someone, sit right here by me"' and footnotes Vanden Heuvel, 'The Sharpest Wit in Washington', The Saturday Evening Post, p. 32 (December 4, 1965). Also gives her dates 12 February 1884 – 20 February 1980, her marriage to Nicholas Longworth in 1906, and her death at 96.

Wikiquote lists 'If you can't say something good about someone, sit right here by me.' under her main Quotes section, cited to Time (9 December 1966), with variants 'If you haven't anything nice to say about anybody, come sit next to me.' and 'If you haven't something good to say about someone sit right here by me.' Intro gives 12 February 1884 – 20 February 1980, only daughter of Theodore Roosevelt.

Dorothy Parker's Wikiquote page has a substantial 'Misattributed' section prefaced by a note that many misquotations are attributed to her — and this quote does not appear anywhere on the page, in any section (verified by full-text search of the page source).

The Theodore Roosevelt Center states: 'At her tea table she kept a pillow which read, "If you can't say something good about someone, sit right here by me."' It also states 'For six decades she hosted a salon at her Dupont Circle home where views were exchanged and deals struck', gives her dates as 1884-1980, her 17 February 1906 White House marriage to Representative Nicholas Longworth of Ohio (Speaker of the House in 1925), and her death at age 96 in 1980.

Professor Buzzkill concludes the quip 'isn't one of hers' (Dorothy Parker's) and states: 'According to the most solid evidence we have, what Alice said (or, more accurately, what she had embroidered on a couch pillow) was "If you can't say something good about someone, sit here by me."'
AZQuotes attributes 'If you don't have anything nice to say, come sit by me.' to Dorothy Parker, tagged under topics including 'Magnolias' — a live example of the misattribution in circulation.
